title: VisuLogic: A Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Reasoning in Multi-modal Large Language Models
claim: The benchmark spans a structured taxonomy of reasoning categories, and current models lag far behind humans on every category.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; nested sunburst beside radar chart
description: The left panel is a two-level sunburst (donut) chart of the benchmark's composition. Inner ring segments are the six main categories: Quantity 35.3% (orange), Spatiality 23.1% (yellow), Position 13.6% (blue), Other 10.8% (dark green), Style 9% (light green) and Attribute 8.2% (pink). The outer ring splits each into subcategories such as Linear Quantity, Rotation and Symmetry, with rotated text labels. The right panel is a hexagonal radar chart with one axis per reasoning category. Four semi-transparent polygons are overlaid: Human in red and extends far out on every axis, while GPT-4o in blue, DeepSeek-R1 in green and Doubao-1.5-vision-pro in yellow cluster near the center. Human peak values are labeled at the vertices, and a legend sits at the bottom right. The eye goes first to the large colorful sunburst, then to the red human polygon.
caption: Composition of the VisuLogic benchmark and performance of representative MLLMs. The left figure shows the distribution of the 6 categories and their subcategories in VisuLogic. The right figure shows accuracies (%) achieved by MLLMs and by human on each category of VisuLogic.
abstract: Visual reasoning is a core component of human intelligence and a critical capability for advanced multimodal models. Yet current reasoning evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often rely on text descriptions and allow language-based reasoning shortcuts, failing to measure genuine vision-centric reasoning. To address this, we introduce VisuLogic: a benchmark of 1,000 human-verified problems across six categories (e.g., quantitative shifts, spatial relations, attribute comparisons). These various types of questions can be evaluated to assess the visual reasoning capabilities of MLLMs from multiple perspectives. We evaluate leading MLLMs on this benchmark and analyze their results to identify common failure modes. Most models score below 30% accuracy-only slightly above the 25% random baseline and far below the 51.4% achieved by humans-revealing significant gaps in visual reasoning. Furthermore, we provide a supplementary training dataset and a reinforcement-learning baseline to support further progress.
